headline: Massachusetts awards more than $13 million for parks, trails and protected land
dek: The grants will support 45 projects, from a new walking-trail network in western Massachusetts to wetland and drinking-water protection on the South Coast and Cape Cod.
body: Massachusetts is directing more than $13 million to 45 projects that will create or improve local parks, expand outdoor access and protect forests, wetlands and water supplies, the Healey-Driscoll administration announced Wednesday. The awards reach from Barnstable and Dennis to the Berkshires and include both public recreation projects and conservation work that may not be open to visitors immediately.

The grants come through three programs run by the Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs: Parkland Acquisitions and Renovations for Communities, known as PARC; Local Acquisitions for Natural Diversity, or LAND; and the Conservation Partnership Grant Program. The [state announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-awards-over-13-million-to-create-improve-local-parks-and-protect-natural-land-across-massachusetts) says PARC helps cities and towns acquire and develop recreation areas, LAND supports conservation commissions protecting natural land, and Conservation Partnership grants help nonprofit land trusts preserve open space.

The project list shows how different those categories can be. The Barnstable Land Trust received $251,650 toward protecting 18 acres at Bridge Creek, next to a town-owned 246-acre conservation area. In Dennis, a $425,000 award will help acquire 5.2 acres at Bakers Pond, where the state says the work will protect habitat, scenic views, sensitive watersheds and drinking-water quality. The Dennis Water District is a project partner and is expected to hold a conservation restriction on the property.

On the South Coast, the Buzzards Bay Coalition received $225,000 for 30 acres along Angeline Brook in Westport and $425,000 for 294 acres at Wings Cove in Marion. The Westport parcel includes 2,028 feet of a cold-water coastal stream that supports native sea-run brook trout, according to the state. The Marion project will conserve coastal wetlands, forests, streams and grasslands while creating opportunities for hiking, wildlife observation and environmental education.

Western Massachusetts projects include $315,000 for 85 acres of forest land at Dry Hill in New Marlborough and $425,000 to protect 82 acres in Westminster that include hay fields, wetlands, a pond and views of Mount Wachusett. In Ashfield, a $72,250 award will support a conservation restriction on 171 acres with forest, beaver-created wetlands and existing snowmobile and hiking trails. The state says those projects can preserve connected habitat while maintaining some agricultural or recreational uses.

One of the largest recreation-focused projects is Cricket Trails in Lanesborough and Hancock. The Trustees of Reservations received $425,000 toward a conservation restriction on 565 acres in a north-south wildlife corridor. The state says the project will create public access to more than 30 miles of free trails for hiking, mountain biking and cross-country skiing, including 10 miles of adaptive mountain-bike trails. The award supports the conservation and public-access work; it does not by itself establish an opening date or guarantee that every planned trail is complete.

The administration framed the grants as climate and public-health infrastructure as well as recreation spending. State officials said parks, forests and natural areas can absorb rainwater that contributes to flooding, provide shade that reduces heat and help protect air and drinking water. Those are broad benefits, however, and the announcement does not quantify how much flooding or heat exposure any individual project will prevent. The immediate, verifiable result is the award of funds to named projects and land-protection partners.

The [Division of Conservation Services program overview](https://www.mass.gov/grant-programs-offered-by-the-division-of-conservation-services) describes the grant system as a way for municipalities and conservation organizations to acquire land, develop parks and renovate recreation facilities. The separate [PARC program page](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/parkland-acquisitions-and-renovations-for-communities-parc-grant-program) says eligible work can include parkland acquisition, new park construction and improvements to existing parks, with award amounts and reimbursement shares varying by project and community.

For residents, the next step will be local implementation: property acquisitions must close, conservation restrictions must be recorded, and park sponsors still have to handle design, permitting, construction, maintenance and access details. Some projects will add places to walk or play; others will mainly keep land, wetlands and water corridors from being developed. Together, the 45 awards show the state using one grant round to pursue both immediate neighborhood recreation and longer-term protection of the landscapes that support New England communities.
